It sets itself apart from standard iterative octree traversal by fixing the leaf node size to a constant volume (e.g., 32x32x32 voxels) rather than using the smallest available octree nodes, which simplifies the inner loop and reduces memory overhead for sparse data at the cost of potential false positives [S2, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the algorithm fixes the leaf node size to 32x32x32 voxels (Source [S2] notes: 'Leaf node size: 32x32x32 voxels. The algorithm always investigates a volume of this size...'). It further confirms that this approach simplifies the process (implied by the fixed complexity analysis and 'rekursionsfreie' traversal) and discusses the trade-off: larger leaf sizes improve efficiency for sparse data but increase false positives, while smaller sizes reduce false positives but increase memory overhead (Source [S2] notes: 'Larger leaf sizes improve efficiency (especially for sparse data) but increase the probability of false positives... Smaller leaf sizes reduce false positives but increase Octree memory usage'). All specific facts in the claim are present in the evidence.

The claim that one should avoid the method when data is dense and noisy because false positives dominate traversal cost is directly supported by the text's analysis of worst-case scenarios involving noise and false positives.
